Note that a named functional call $\f(\Cs)$ may invoke a dotted method
declaration if the declaration is provided by the trait or object
enclosing the call.  To account for this, let $\Cs_0$ be the trait or
object declaration immediately enclosing the call.
%
Then we consider a named functional call $\f(\Cs)$ as $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$
if $\Cs_0$ provides dotted method declarations applicable to $\f(\Cs)$, and
use the rule for applicability to dotted method calls (described in
\secref{dotted-method-applicability}) to determine which declarations
are applicable to $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$.



\section{Applicability to Dotted Method Calls}
\seclabel{dotted-method-applicability}

Dotted method applications can be characterized similarly to named
functional applications, except that, analogously to dotted method declarations,
we use $\Cs_0$ to denote the dynamic type of the receiver object,
and, as for named functional calls, $\Cs$ to denote the dynamic
type of the argument of a  dotted method call.
We write $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$ to refer to the  call.

A dotted method declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{applicable}
to a dotted method call $\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$ if $\Cs_0 \Ovrsubtype
\Ps_0$ and $\Cs \Ovrsubtype \Ps$.
If the types $\Ps_0$ and $\Ps$ include static parameters,
they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference}
before checking the applicability of the declaration to the call.



\section{Applicability for Functionals with Varargs and Keyword Parameters}
\seclabel{applicability-with-special-params}

The basic idea for handling varargs and keyword
parameters is that we
can think of a functional declaration that has such parameters as
though it were (possibly infinitely) many declarations, one for each
set of arguments it may be called with.  In other words, we expand
these declarations so that there exists a declaration for each number
of arguments that can be passed to it.


A declaration with a varargs parameter corresponds to an infinite
number of declarations, one for every number of arguments that may be
passed to the varargs parameter.  In practice, we can bound that
number by the maximum number of arguments that the functional is
called with anywhere in the program (in other words, a given program
will contain only a finite number of calls with different numbers of
arguments).  The expansion described here is a conceptual one to
simplify the description of the semantics; we do not expect a real
implementation to actually expand these declarations at compile time.
%
For example, the following declaration:
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z : ZZ...):ZZ
\begin{Fortress}
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}\ldots)\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)
\end{Fortress}
would be expanded into:
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ):ZZ
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z1 : ZZ):ZZ
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z1 : ZZ, z2 : ZZ):ZZ
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z1 : ZZ, z2 : ZZ, z3 : ZZ):ZZ
%...
\begin{Fortress}
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{2} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{2} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{3} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
\(\ldots\)
\end{Fortress}
A declaration with a varargs parameter is applicable to a call if
any one of the expanded declarations is applicable.

\seclabel{resolving-overloading}

To evaluate a given functional call,
it is necessary to determine which functional declaration
to dispatch to.
To do so,
we consider the declarations that are applicable to that call at run time.
If there is exactly one such declaration,
then the call dispatches to that declaration.
If there is no such declaration,
then the call is \emph{undefined}, which is a static error.
(However, see \secref{applicability-with-coercion}
for how coercion may add to the set of applicable declarations.)
If multiple declarations are applicable to the call at run time,
then we choose an arbitrary declaration among the declarations such that
no other applicable declaration is more specific than them.



We use the subtype relation to compare parameter types to determine
a more specific declaration.
Formally, a declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more specific} than a declaration
$\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$.  Similarly, a declaration
$\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is more specific than a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$
if $\Ps_0 \strictsubtype \Qs_0$ and $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$.
(See \secref{resolving-coercion} for how coercion
changes the definition of ``more specific''.)
Restrictions on the definition of overloaded functionals
(see \chapref{overloaded-declarations})
guarantee that among all applicable declarations,
one is more specific than all the others.
If the declarations include static parameters,
they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference}
before comparing their parameter types
to determine which declaration is more specific.

## Setting up a batch's worktrees

The workflow script cannot touch the filesystem before its first agent runs, so
the coordinator creates the worktrees and pushes the empty branches first, from
the commit `main` is at, which is then the script's `args.base`:

```sh
cd /home/user/fortress && BASE=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
for r in r1-atomic-static r2-literal-wrap; do
  git worktree add -b wip/repair-$r /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*} main
  cp -a ProjectFortress/build /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*}/ProjectFortress/   # javac incremental; scalac rebuilds anyway
  mkdir -p /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*}/tmp
  git push -u origin wip/repair-$r
done
```

Copy the build, never symlink it: a symlinked build makes `ProjectProperties`
resolve every cache path to the main tree (`batched-climb-plan.md` §4). After
the batch lands, the commit stage removes the worktrees and local branches; the
remote `wip/` branches are deleted in the GitHub UI.

# probe <dir> <name> <link-flag-sets...>: link under each flag set, run after the last if a jar exists
probe () { local d=$1 p=$2; shift 2
  for fl in "$@"; do
    echo "=== fortress link $p.fss   $fl"
    rm -f $FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache/$p.jar $FORTRESS_CACHES/analyzed_cache/$p-*; touch $d/$p.fss

  done
  if [ -f $FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache/$p.jar ]; then
    echo "=== fortress run $p"
    timeout 300 java -Xmx1g -cp "$RCP" com.sun.fortress.runtimeSystem.MainWrapper $p 2>&1 | grep -v '^\s*at \|^\s*\.\.\. [0-9]* more' | cut -c1-400 | head -40
    echo "run exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
  fi
}
EOF
echo ok

component ScopeArms
export Executable

(* MieDispatchSub with arms that can be told apart: the Tag generic returns a TagM, the
   Sub generic a SubM, both Markers.  The Sub generic names its parameter Y, so the
   dispatcher must rename it to the Tag generic's X.  Through b: Tag[Blue] the call is
   checked as the Tag generic at X = Blue and dispatched; the specification's answer is
   TagM[Blue] for Mixed (Sub[Blue] does not apply), SubM[Blue] for SubBlue, TagM[Blue] for
   TagBlue.  Mixed needs the relaxed checkP to link. *)
trait Tag[\X\] end
trait Sub[\X\] extends Tag[\X\] end
object Red end
object Blue end
object Mixed extends { Sub[\Red\], Tag[\Blue\] } end
object SubBlue extends Sub[\Blue\] end
object TagBlue extends Tag[\Blue\] end
trait Marker[\X\] end
object TagM[\X\] extends Marker[\X\] end
object SubM[\X\] extends Marker[\X\] end

grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\]): Marker[\X\] = TagM[\X\]
grab[\Y\](t: Sub[\Y\]): Marker[\Y\] = SubM[\Y\]

name(m: Any): String = typecase m of
    TagM[\Red\] => "TagM[Red]"
    TagM[\Blue\] => "TagM[Blue]"
    SubM[\Red\] => "SubM[Red]"
    SubM[\Blue\] => "SubM[Blue]"
    else => "other"
  end

run(): () = do
  r: Sub[\Red\] = Mixed
  println("grab(r), r: Sub[Red] = Mixed    -> " name(grab(r)))
  b1: Tag[\Blue\] = Mixed
  println("grab(b1), b1: Tag[Blue] = Mixed   -> " name(grab(b1)))
  b2: Tag[\Blue\] = SubBlue
  println("grab(b2), b2: Tag[Blue] = SubBlue -> " name(grab(b2)))
  b3: Tag[\Blue\] = TagBlue
  println("grab(b3), b3: Tag[Blue] = TagBlue -> " name(grab(b3)))
end
end
EOF

export Executable

(* The ZZ32 naming defect reached through a generic dispatcher, with no multiple
   instantiation: IntSub is a Sub[ZZ32] only.  Through t: Tag[ZZ32] the call is checked as
   the Tag generic at X = ZZ32 and dispatched, and the Sub arm applies. *)
trait Tag[\X\] end
trait Sub[\X\] extends Tag[\X\] end
object IntSub extends Sub[\ZZ32\] end
trait Marker[\X\] end
object TagM[\X\] extends Marker[\X\] end
object SubM[\X\] extends Marker[\X\] end

grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\]): Marker[\X\] = TagM[\X\]
grab[\X\](t: Sub[\X\]): Marker[\X\] = SubM[\X\]

run(): () = do
  t: Tag[\ZZ32\] = IntSub
  println("grab(t), t: Tag[ZZ32] = IntSub -> " (typecase grab(t) of

end
end

cat > ScopeAlpha2.fss <<'EOF'
component ScopeAlpha2
export Executable

(* Two static parameters, named in the opposite order by the more specific generic:
   pair[\B,A\](t: SubTwo[\B,A\]) is pair[\A,B\](t: SubTwo[\A,B\]) up to renaming.
   Through t: Two[\Red,Blue\] the call is checked as the Two generic at A = Red, B = Blue. *)
trait Two[\A,B\] end
trait SubTwo[\A,B\] extends Two[\A,B\] end
object Red end
object Blue end
object RB extends SubTwo[\Red,Blue\] end
object PlainRB extends Two[\Red,Blue\] end
trait Marker[\A,B\] end
object TwoM[\A,B\] extends Marker[\A,B\] end
object SubM[\A,B\] extends Marker[\A,B\] end

pair[\A,B\](t: Two[\A,B\]): Marker[\A,B\] = TwoM[\A,B\]
pair[\B,A\](t: SubTwo[\B,A\]): Marker[\B,A\] = SubM[\B,A\]

name(m: Any): String = typecase m of
    TwoM[\Red,Blue\] => "TwoM[Red,Blue]"
    SubM[\Red,Blue\] => "SubM[Red,Blue]"
    else => "other"
  end

run(): () = do
  t1: Two[\Red,Blue\] = RB
  println("pair(t1), t1: Two[Red,Blue] = RB      -> " name(pair(t1)))
  t2: Two[\Red,Blue\] = PlainRB
  println("pair(t2), t2: Two[Red,Blue] = PlainRB -> " name(pair(t2)))
end
end
EOF

input.command:
cd /home/user/fortress/ProjectFortress && python3 - <<'EOF'
import re, glob, os, collections
out = []
for dirn in ['compiler_tests']:
    for f in sorted(glob.glob(dirn + '/*.fss')):
        src = open(f, encoding='utf-8', errors='replace').read()
        src = re.sub(r'\(\*.*?\*\)', '', src, flags=re.S)
        decls = collections.defaultdict(list)
        for m in re.finditer(r'^[ \t]*(?:private\s+|getter\s+|setter\s+)?([a-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*|[A-Z][A-Z_]+|opr\s+\S+)\s*(\[\\[^\]]*\\\])?\s*\(', src, re.M):
            name = m.group(1)
            if name in ('if','while','for','println','print','do','case','typecase','assert','fail','label','exit','throw','atomic','spawn','run','end'): continue
            decls[name].append(bool(m.group(2)))
        hits = [n for n, g in decls.items() if len(g) >= 2 and any(g)]
        if hits:
            out.append((os.path.basename(f), hits))
for f, h in out: print(f, ' '.join(h[:6]))
print(len(out))
EOF

# Triage

**The short answer.** zero.md's 173 was taken with `checkP` relaxed *broadly* — its switch sits inside `pExcInner`, which the overloading
checker's exclusion certificate also reaches — and it is a lower bound: a memo in the overloading checker hides 27 to 35 errors depending
on the build. Checked in every context there are **203**. None of them goes away with a weaker exclusion relation. Batch 3's *narrow* placement
makes things worse: **487**. By class: 35 are refused by the specification's static-parameter sentence, 56 by the Meet Rule, 29 are library
defects, 79 are `fill`'s shape (a type variable against an arrow parameter), 4 are a checker capture defect. Eleven api lines take the 203 to
179, eleven more to 81, two more and a rename to 72. **Batch 3 should declare 41, or 40 with the closure's accommodation, not 2.**

## 1. The two copies, reproduced, and why the count moves

* **Everything applied** (ZALL3, `-Dprobe.zero.dropP -Dprobe.zero.eligibleNarrow`, zero's classes): **173**, twice, identical lists
  (`triage/counts.txt`, r01, r06). **Batch 3 as written** (ZL, `dropP` only): **45**, zero's ZLP 44 plus the `:411` closure error (r02).
* **zero's switch is the broad placement.** It returns `pFalse()` from `checkP` inside `pExcInner` (`shadow.patch`, the `checkP` hunk; tree
  `types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:443-456`), and the overloading certificate lands there: `OverloadingOracle.excludes` is "the meet of the two domains
  is Bottom" (`overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:190-194`), and the meet is Bottom when `normConjunct` finds two excluding conjuncts
  (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:632-640`). The narrow placement had never been run against the overloading rule.
* **The count depends on the build, not only on the library.** The same copy and switches give 173 (zero's classes), 170 (the same
  sources plus this probe's switch, all off), 176 (plus the triage `OverloadingChecker`), 175 and 168 (with the diagnostics on); each build
  repeats its own number exactly (r01/r06, r03/r16). Only `fill`, `generate`, `map` and `copy` move. The cause is `validOverloadingMemo`
  (`typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:441-462`): it caches a `true` per *pair of declarations* (key `:452`), but a pair inherited by several
  traits is checked once per trait, each in its own instantiation (`:282-320`), in hash-set order. A pair valid in one trait's context is
  then taken as valid in the next. With the tree's own switch `-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false` (`:77`) every build gives **203**
  (r20, r21, r25 byte-identical), a superset of every memo-on list; the classification is of the 203. Hence `shadow.patch` stays as it is:
  any edit to the shadow reshuffles the memo-on count (r26), and zero's captures reproduce only from it alone.

18:So on (H) the specification settles it against the compiled checker's `checkP` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:443-456`) and against the two hierarchy questions that enforce it (`scala_src/typechecker/TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:178`, `:187`). The worker's four errors on the MinP shape (`probes/test-preedit.txt:2-10`) are that enforcement.
38:2. **"Drop it together with enforcing `overloading.tex:100-105`" over-states what soundness needs.** The hole is the Return Type Rule check trusting one instantiation (`OverloadingOracle.scala:88-95`). The sentence closes it, but the sentence is a restriction on every overload set, generic-beside-generic included, and its cost was left unmeasured by the worker (REPORT.md, "What this does not settle", third item). Measured here by a column-0 grep for a declaration `name[\...\](` beside `name(` in the same file (functional methods and nested declarations not counted, so a lower bound): `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/Compiled12.invariantInference.fss:52-61` (run by its `.test`) and `compiler_tests/Compiled6.ak.fss:14-15` (a bare `.fss`; whether the suite runs it was not checked); `library_tests/` 0; `LibraryBuiltin/` 0, so the compiler prelude has none; the interpreter's library `Library/Generator2.fss:52-57` (`takeleft[\T\](a: Nothing[\T\], b: Any)` beside `takeleft(a: Any, b: Any)`, and `takeright` the same); and in the interpreter's gated `tests/`, `overloadTest8.fss:33-37`, `doubledOverloading.fss:36-41`, `GeneratorNullPointer.fss:18-20`, `ArrayListQuick.fss:36-55` and `PureListQuick.fss`. Every one of these return types is `String`, `()`, `ZZ32` or the parameter-free `Any`: none mentions the generic's parameter, so none has the hole, and the sentence would refuse all of them for no soundness. This is the measured cost that makes the sentence Pavol's and not a repair worker's.
40:3. **The interpreter's rule is narrower than the worker reads it.** `OverloadedFunction.java:496-498` refuses a pair when a symbolic type was seen or a parameter pair is *unrelated* and nothing excludes; `walk` accepts `Library/Generator2.fss:52-57` and `tests/GeneratorNullPointer.fss:18-20`, both one-generic-one-not, both subtype-related in every position. The worker's table cell "interpreter: refused" is measured for the `Tag[\X\]` beside `Tag[\ZZ32\]` shape (`probes/walk-ProbeMIEPickCtl.txt:5-6`) and must not be generalised to every specialised overload. The error text itself says what the test is: "unrelated (neither subtype, excludes, nor equal) and no excluding pair is present" (`probes/probe-overload.txt:39`).
48:Rule 4 of the brief: the specification answers a divergence; a silent specification is the reason to think harder, not to stop. The specification here is not silent. On the divergence "`pick[\X\]` beside `pick`: compiled accepts, `walk` refuses" it sides with `walk` (`overloading.tex:100-105`), which is rule 4's first outcome, repair. The repair is the sentence, and the sentence is what the batch record reserved to Pavol before this rung ran (`CLIMB-BATCH-3.md:18`; `triage.md:113`, "(b) is Pavol's decision about the specification, not a patch: the 35, and the sentence's reach over overrides"). It was reserved because the library the route makes the standard uses shapes the sentence refuses (the triage's 35 sites; `Library/Generator2.fss:52-57` in this ruling), and `POSITIONS.md:39` makes the library's practice the standard. A judge does not lift a reservation the coordinator wrote into the record Pavol launched with "go".
75:(a) **The specification's sentence** (`overloading.tex:100-108`): overloads of a name share their static parameters; a call site instantiates them once. This is triage decision (b). Closes the hole; makes the run-time choice of instantiation moot on the checker's side. Cost: refuses the corpus sites of section 3 item 2 — `compiler_tests/Compiled12.invariantInference.fss:52-61`, `Compiled6.ak.fss:14-15`, `Library/Generator2.fss:52-57`, four interpreter tests — none of which has the hole; the triage's 35 library sites, already errors today, then need renames rather than a checker accommodation; and the reading of "static parameters" for functional methods of generic traits must be fixed (`triage.md:57-59`), or the sentence refuses overrides. Deleting or rewriting gated tests is itself a reserved stop (`PLAN.md:52`), so this choice carries that cost explicitly.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Library copies for the zero probe.  usage: make-lib.py <dir>

L0    the tree's library, copied unchanged (the control)
P3a   `excludes Condition[\()\]` dropped, nothing else (the trace's L1a half)
P3b   P3a + the first ANDCOND's parameter arrows narrowed to `I->Boolean`
P3c   P3a + the second ANDCOND (.fss:4467) deleted
ZP    the four untyped local-function parameters written out (piece 1)
ZL    the batch-3 L rung's five plain api defects
ZLP   ZL + ZP, the excludes clause KEPT (isolates what piece 3's repair costs)
ZALL  ZL + ZP + the P3d repair
ZALL2 ZALL with Array3's plane(k) left untyped -- still crashes, so the crash is not plane's
ZALL3 ZALL + a declared return type () on the three local functions -- the one that reaches
      zero crashes
P3dx  P3d with a println in each branch of andCondCombine, to see which branch fires
"""
import os, re, shutil, sys, io

S = sys.argv[1]
FILES = ["Library/FortressLibrary.fss", "Library/FortressLibrary.fsi",
         "Library/RangeInternals.fsi", "Library/List.fsi"]
VARIANTS = ("L0", "P3a", "P3b", "P3c", "P3d", "ZP", "ZL", "ZLP", "ZALL", "ZALL2", "ZALL3", "P3dx")
for v in VARIANTS:
    os.makedirs(f"{S}/{v}", exist_ok=True)
    for p in FILES:
        shutil.copy(p, f"{S}/{v}/{os.path.basename(p)}")

def edit(path, subs):
    s = io.open(path, encoding="utf-8").read()
    for a, b, n in subs:
        assert s.count(a) == n, (path, a[:60], s.count(a), n)
        s = s.replace(a, b)
    io.open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8").write(s)

# ---- piece 3: the excludes clause (FortressLibrary.fsi:2526 / .fss:4444) ------
EC = ("trait RelationalPredicateCondition[\\E\\] extends { Condition[\\()\\] } excludes Condition[\\()\\]",
      "trait RelationalPredicateCondition[\\E\\] extends { Condition[\\()\\] }", 1)
# the first ANDCOND (.fss:1248, .fsi:801): its parameter arrows return Condition[\()\]
AC_OLD = "opr ANDCOND[\\I\\](p1:I->Condition[\\()\\], p2:I->Condition[\\()\\]): I->Condition[\\()\\]"
AC_NEW = "opr ANDCOND[\\I\\](p1:I->Boolean, p2:I->Boolean): I->Condition[\\()\\]"
# the second ANDCOND (.fss:4467), one line, .fss only
AC2 = ("""(* combining two relational predicates into a new relational predicate *)
opr ANDCOND[\\E\\](p : Generator[\\ E \\] -> RelationalPredicateCondition[\\ E \\] , q : Generator[\\ E \\] -> RelationalPredicateCondition[\\ E \\] ) : Generator[\\ E \\] -> Condition[\\ () \\] = (fn (x : Generator[\\ E \\]) : AndRelationalPredicateCondition[\\ E \\] => AndRelationalPredicateCondition[\\ E \\](p, q, x))
""", "", 1)

# ---- piece 1: the four untyped local-function parameters ----------------------
P1 = [("    body(i): L = r.lift((o.body)(i))",
       "    body(i:I): L = r.lift((o.body)(i))", 1),
      ("""  getter asString(): String = do
    r : String := "[" b0 "#" s0 "," b1 "#" s1 "]"
    row(i) =""",
       """  getter asString(): String = do
    r : String := "[" b0 "#" s0 "," b1 "#" s1 "]"
    row(i:ZZ32) =""", 1)]

def p1_array3(s):
    # Array3's asString (.fss:2678): two local functions, three untyped parameters
    for a, b in (("      row(i,k) =", "      row(i:ZZ32,k:ZZ32) ="),
                 ("      plane(k) =", "      plane(k:ZZ32) =")):
        assert s.count(a) == 1, (a, s.count(a))

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""routeC-count.py <lib-stack dir> <tracked FortressLibrary.fsi>: summarise the three
WorldFlip runs of dispatch-run.sh section 4 (wf-off.out, wf-all.out, wf-ret.out): the
whole-unit and per-api error counts, the return type rule errors, and every distinct pair
the route C sketch refused (its @@ROUTEC lines), grouped by the generic declaration and by
the trait that declares the specialised one.  The library copy (make-lib.py's ZALL3) has
the tracked file's line numbers up to line 600, where every refused pair lies."""
import re, sys, collections
L, FSI = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
src = open(FSI, encoding="utf-8").read().split("\n")
def text(line): return src[line - 1].strip()
def owner(line):
    for i in range(line - 1, -1, -1):
        m = re.match(r'(?:value )?(?:trait|object) (\w+)', src[i])
        if m: return m.group(1)
def span(s): return s.split('/')[-1]
def line(s): return int(span(s).split(':')[1])
def rtr(t): return set(re.findall(r'the return type of .*? @ (\S+) should be a subtype of the\n\s*return type of .*? @ (\S+)', t))
runs = {}
for mode in ("off", "all", "ret"):
    t = open(f"{L}/wf-{mode}.out", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").read()
    pairs = set()
    for l in t.splitlines():
        m = re.match(r'@@ROUTEC (\S+) .*?  BESIDE  (\S+) ', l)
        if m: pairs.add((span(m.group(1)), span(m.group(2))))
    runs[mode] = dict(total=re.findall(r'File \S+ has (\d+) errors?', t)[-1],
                      apis=re.findall(r'checkApi (\S+) -> errors=(\d+)', t),
                      rtr={(span(a), span(b)) for a, b in rtr(t)}, pairs=pairs,
                      secs=re.findall(r'ELAPSED (\d+) s', t)[-1])
off_rtr = runs["off"]["rtr"]
print("# Route C's overload half over the interpreter's library: WorldFlip on make-lib.py's ZALL3 copy with")
print("# -Dprobe.zero.dropP=true -Dprobe.zero.eligibleNarrow=true (the zero probe's stack) and -Dprobe.routeC=<mode>.")
print("# mode  whole-unit errors  FortressLibrary api  return-type-rule errors  refused pairs (of them already refused by the stock rule)  secs")
for mode, r in runs.items():
    api = dict(r["apis"]).get("FortressLibrary")
    print(f"  {mode:4}  {r['total']:>17}  {api:>19}  {len(r['rtr']):>23}  {len(r['pairs']):>13} ({len(r['pairs'] & off_rtr)})  {r['secs']}")
for mode in ("ret", "all"):
    pairs = sorted(runs[mode]["pairs"], key=lambda p: (line(p[1]), line(p[0])))
    print(f"\n## -Dprobe.routeC={mode}: {len(pairs)} refused pairs, all declared in FortressLibrary.fsi")
    print("# by the generic declaration: its line, its text, the number of specialisations refused beside it")

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""sentence-scan.py <mode own|lifted> <file...>: pairs of same-named declarations whose static
parameters differ (Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-105), found from the text.  Groups the
names the compiled overloading checker examines: top-level functions with the functional methods
(declarations with a `self` parameter inside a trait or object), and each trait's or object's own
dotted methods (inherited ones are not seen).  Local functions are not overloads the checker
examines and are skipped (indented deeper than the enclosing block's members).  Symbolic operators
are listed apart, because the checker skips them (NodeUtil.validOp).  Static parameters are compared
by count, kind and bounds after positional renaming.  Prints one line per pair: file:line:line name."""
import re, sys, itertools
mode, files = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2:]
DECL = re.compile(r'^(\s*)(?:(?:private|abstract|getter|setter|override|value|coerce)\s+)*'
                  r'(opr\s+(?:BIG\s+)?(?:\S+?)|[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_\']*)\s*(\[\\.*?\\\])?\s*\((.*)$')
TO = re.compile(r'^(\s*)(?:value\s+)?(trait|object)\s+([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)\s*(\[\\.*?\\\])?')
KEYW = {'if','while','for','do','case','typecase','label','exit','throw','atomic','spawn','then','else',
        'elif','end','println','print','assert','fail','try','catch','fn','of','in','also','at'}
def strip_comments(s):
    out, depth, i = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(s):
        if s.startswith('(*', i): depth += 1; i += 2; continue
        if depth and s.startswith('*)', i): depth -= 1; i += 2; continue
        if depth == 0 or s[i] == '\n': out.append(s[i])
        i += 1
    return ''.join(out)
def sparams(txt):
    if not txt: return []
    inner = txt[2:-2]
    parts, d, cur = [], 0, ''
    for ch in inner:
        if ch in '[(': d += 1
        if ch in '])': d -= 1
        if ch == ',' and d == 0: parts.append(cur.strip()); cur = ''
        else: cur += ch
    if cur.strip(): parts.append(cur.strip())
    res = []
    for p in parts:
        m = re.match(r'(nat|int|bool|dim|unit|opr)\s+(\S+)(.*)', p)
        kind, name, rest = (m.group(1), m.group(2), m.group(3)) if m else ('type', p.split()[0], p[len(p.split()[0]):])
        b = re.sub(r'^\s*extends\s*', '', rest).strip().strip('{}').strip()
        b = '' if b in ('', 'Any') else b
        res.append((kind, name, b))
    return res
def differ(p, q):
    if len(p) != len(q) or any(a[0] != b[0] for a, b in zip(p, q)): return True
    ren = {b[1]: a[1] for a, b in zip(p, q)}
    def r(t): return re.sub(r'\b[A-Za-z_]\w*\b', lambda m: ren.get(m.group(0), m.group(0)), t)
    return any(a[2].replace(' ', '') != r(b[2]).replace(' ', '') for a, b in zip(p, q))
def valid_op(n):   # NodeUtil.validOp for the opr names the checker examines
    if n in ('juxtaposition','in','per','square','cubic','inverse','squared','cubed'): return True
    if n in ('SUM','PROD') or len(n) < 2 or n.startswith('_') or n.endswith('_'): return False
    return all(c == '_' or c.isupper() for c in n)
for f in files:
    lines = strip_comments(open(f, encoding='utf-8', errors='replace').read()).split('\n')
    groups = {}          # (scope, name) -> [(line, sparams, symbolic)]
    scope, sp_trait, member_ind = None, [], None
    for i, l in enumerate(lines, 1):
        if not l.strip(): continue
        ind = len(l) - len(l.lstrip())
        m = TO.match(l)
        if m and ind == 0:
            scope, sp_trait, member_ind = m.group(3), sparams(m.group(4)), None
            if re.search(r'\bend\s*$', l): scope = None
            continue
        if ind == 0 and re.match(r'end\b', l.strip()): scope = None; continue
        if ind == 0 and scope is not None and not l.startswith(' '): scope = None
        m = DECL.match(l)
        if not m: continue
        name = m.group(2)
        if name in KEYW: continue
        rest = m.group(4)
        if scope is None:
            if ind != 0: continue
        else:
            if member_ind is None: member_ind = ind
            if ind != member_ind: continue
        is_opr = name.startswith('opr')
        base = re.sub(r'^opr\s+(BIG\s+)?', '', name)
        symbolic = is_opr and not valid_op(base)
        # a declaration has a return type, a body, or ends the api line; a call does neither
        if not re.search(r'\)\s*(:|=|$|throws|requires|ensures|end\b)', rest) and not rest.rstrip().endswith(','):
            continue
        own = sparams(m.group(3))
        functional = scope is not None and re.search(r'\bself\b', rest.split(')')[0] + ')')
        if scope is None or functional:
            key = (None, base)
            spl = (sp_trait + own) if (functional and mode == 'lifted') else own
        else:
            key = (scope, base); spl = own
        groups.setdefault(key, []).append((i, spl, symbolic))
    for (sc, n), ds in sorted(groups.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1][0][0]):
        for (a, pa, sa), (b, pb, sb) in itertools.combinations(ds, 2):
            if differ(pa, pb):
                tag = 'SYMBOLIC ' if (sa or sb) else ''
                print(f"{f}:{a}:{b}\t{tag}{n}" + (f"\t(in {sc})" if sc else ''))
EOF

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

  (cd $a && unzip -qo "$1" 2>/dev/null); (cd $b && unzip -qo "$2" 2>/dev/null)
  local d=$(diff -rq $a $b | sed -e "s#$a#A#g; s#$b#B#g")
  [ -z "$d" ] && echo "identical ($(find $a -type f | wc -l) files)" || echo "DIFFERENT: $(echo "$d" | wc -l) files"

probe () { local d=$1 p=$2; shift 2               # probe <dir> <name> <flag sets...>
  for fl in "$@"; do

      echo "run exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
    fi
  done; }
MIE="-Dprobe.rungP=hier"
{ for s in off callsite skip; do
    for p in MieDispatch MieDispatchSub MieDispatchAny; do probe $M $p "$MIE -Dprobe.scope=$s"; done

for p in ScopeArms ScopeMethod; do

for p in ScopeZZ32Sub ScopeAlpha2; do
  { for s in off callsite; do probe $D $p "-Dprobe.scope=$s"; done; } > $D/$p.compiled.txt 2>&1; done

J=$W/javap; rm -rf $J; mkdir -p $J

  for s in off callsite; do echo; echo "## $s"
    javap -c -p $J/$s.class | sed -n '/the_function(/,/^$/p' | grep -v '^\s*$' | cut -c1-230; done
} > $D/javap-template.txt

      (cd ProjectFortress/compiler_tests && java -Xmx4g -Xss64m $FL -Dfortress.caches=$C -cp $CLS$CP \

        (cd ProjectFortress/compiler_tests && java -Xmx1g -cp "$R" com.sun.fortress.runtimeSystem.MainWrapper $p 2>&1 \
           | grep -v '^\s*at \|^\s*\.\.\. [0-9]* more' | cut -c1-300 | head -30; echo "run exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"); fi; } > $O/$p.txt 2>&1
  done; }

{ echo "# compiler_tests declaring a generic overload, or matching 'overload' or Generic/Overload in the name: $(wc -l < $LIST)"
  echo "# test | stock link/run exits | callsite: output, classes | skip: output"
  for p in $(cat $LIST); do
    o=$(cmp -s $W/tests-stock/$p.txt $W/tests-callsite/$p.txt && echo same || echo DIFF)
    k=$(cmp -s $W/tests-stock/$p.txt $W/tests-skip/$p.txt && echo same || echo DIFF)
    if [ -f $W/tests-stock/$p.jar ]; then j=$(cmpjar $W/tests-stock/$p.jar $W/tests-callsite/$p.jar); else j="no jar"; fi

  done
  echo; echo "# skip's differing output"; for p in $(cat $LIST); do cmp -s $W/tests-stock/$p.txt $W/tests-skip/$p.txt || diff $W/tests-stock/$p.txt $W/tests-skip/$p.txt | head -8; done
} > $D/compiler-tests.txt

# ----------------- 4. the sentence over the interpreter's library: the zero probe's stack
N=explorations/perf-probes/nat; Z=$N/zero; P=explorations/perf-probes/prelude; L=$W/lib-stack; mkdir -p $L
rm -rf $L/shadow-src $L/jshadow-src $L/oc-src; R=com/sun/fortress
for rel in scala_src/typechecker/Formula.scala scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala scala_src/types/TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala \
           scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala scala_src/typechecker/ExportChecker.scala scala_src/typechecker/TypeWellFormedChecker.scala \

prelude $W/caches -cp $CP
prelude $W/caches-cs -Dprobe.scope=callsite -cp $W/classes:$CP

  (cd $a && unzip -qo "$1" 2>/dev/null); (cd $b && unzip -qo "$2" 2>/dev/null)

  [ -z "$d" ] && echo "identical ($(find $a -type f | wc -l) files)" || echo "DIFFERENT: $(echo "$d" | wc -l) files"
  rm -rf $a $b; }
{ echo "# the compiler prelude compiled stock and with -Dprobe.scope=callsite"

       com.sun.fortress.Shell link $p.fss 2>&1 | sed -e "s#$PWD/##g"; exit ${PIPESTATUS[0]}); echo "link exit=$?"
    if [ -f $FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache/$p.jar ]; then

{ echo "# compiler_tests declaring a generic overload, or matching 'overload' or Generic/Overload in the name: $(wc -l < $LIST)"

  for p in $(cat $LIST); do

    echo "$p | $(grep -h 'exit=' $W/tests-stock/$p.txt | tr '\n' ' ')| callsite: output $o, classes $j | skip: output $k"
  done
  echo; echo "# skip's differing output"; for p in $(cat $LIST); do cmp -s $W/tests-stock/$p.txt $W/tests-skip/$p.txt || diff $W/tests-stock/$p.txt $W/tests-skip/$p.txt | head -8; done

# The dispatcher taking the call site's static arguments: sized in a shadow

**The answer.** The generic dispatcher is already loaded under the call site's static arguments; only its arms ignore them. Making each generic arm use the dispatcher's own static parameters is one file, one edited function and three new helpers: 43 code lines in `OverloadSet.java`, plus 1 for the switch and 3 for the variant that leaves generic arms out of a dispatcher that has no static parameters. `MieDispatchSub` then prints `Marker[Blue]`. The compiler prelude is byte-identical, and so are the classes of 40 of the 43 compiler tests that declare generic overloads. The other 3 differ only inside a generic dispatcher, and all 43 print the same. Top-level functions only: generic dotted methods fail the same way and are not covered (`ScopeMethod`).

## 1. How the compiled path handles generics today

- A **static argument** is the type that fills a generic's static parameter at one use. In `grab[\Blue\](b)` it is `Blue`. Usually nobody writes it: the checker infers it from the declared types at the call, so `b: Tag[\Blue\]` gives `X = Blue` (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:912-930`).
- An **instantiation** is the generic with its static parameters replaced by static arguments: `grab[\Blue\]` is an instantiation of `grab[\X\]`.
- The compiler writes one *template* class per generic function, with `X` left in the names of the types it mentions (`Marker⟦X⟧`). The class loader stamps an instantiation from it when a class named with real arguments is first needed. For `grab⟦Blue⟧` it copies the template and rewrites every `X` in it to `Blue` (`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java`, `MethodInstantiater.java`). The part of the name after `✚`, the template's arrow type, is never rewritten (`InstantiationMap.java:354`).
- A call that needs no choice at run time is compiled as a call to that named class. The checker's static arguments go straight into the name (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:3670-3735`), so `grab(z)` with `z: Tag[\ZZ32\]` calls `grab⟦ZZ32⟧`.
- **Dispatch** is choosing at run time which declaration of an overloaded name runs, by the argument's actual type. A **dispatcher** is the method the compiler generates for that. It tests the argument against each declaration, most specific first, and calls the first that applies (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1303-1760`). One is generated for a declaration when some more specific declaration of the same name may apply at run time. If the least specific declaration is generic, the dispatcher is itself a template, named and loaded like any generic function: `grab⟦Blue⟧` at the call site (`OverloadSet.java:2005-2062`).
- **RTTI** (run-time type information) is the object every compiled value carries that describes its type. That includes the argument of each generic supertype, one per generic name: `Mixed`'s RTTI says `Sub` of `Red` and `Tag` of `Blue`.
- How a generic arm finds its static arguments today: it asks the value for its RTTI (`getRTTI`), asks that for the argument at the arm's generic (`Sub__1()`, giving `Red`), and passes the answer to `RTHelpers.loadClosureClass`. That call spells the instance's name from the RTTI's own Java class (`runtimeSystem/RTHelpers.java:160-178`, `runtimeValues/RTTI.java:53-58`), and the loader stamps it (`OverloadSet.java:1410-1728`). Inside a dispatcher template the arms do this too: they ignore the template's `X`, which the loader has already set to the call site's argument (`../javap-excerpts.txt:60-72`).
- The authors weighed the question in a comment: "Some overloads have static args, but even if they are supplied, runtime inference is still necessary (so I think) -- drc 2010-02-24 / Not quite so -- if each static parameter is mentioned in any invariant occurrence, then the supplied type is exact" (`OverloadSet.java:1981-1990`).

## 2. The design

**What the specification says.** Declarations of one name share their static parameters (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-105`), so "static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable" (`:106-107`). The chapter assumes "that all static variables in functional calls have been instantiated or inferred" (`:136-138`), and they are "statically inferred from the context of the function call" (`expressions/var-ref.tex:37-40`). One set of static arguments, fixed at the call, therefore applies to every declaration. A declaration applies at run time if the value's type is a subtype of its parameter type at those arguments. For `MieDispatchSub`, `grab(b)` with `b: Tag[\Blue\]` fixes `X = Blue`. `Mixed` is not a `Sub[\Blue\]`, so the `Tag` declaration runs and the answer is `Marker[Blue]`.

**`MieDispatchAny`'s `grab(a)`, `a: Any`.** The specification refuses the program: `grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])` beside `grab(a: Any)` is "one declaration [with] static parameters and another [without] them" (`overloading.tex:103-105`). The question of which declaration runs therefore does not arise. If the sentence is not enforced, both readings give the same answer. The call was resolved to `grab(Any)`, which has no static parameters, so the call site supplies none. With no arguments to instantiate it, the generic declaration is not applicable. The code should refuse the pair at compile time (§5). Failing that, it should leave the generic arm out of such a dispatcher, which is the `skip` variant below. Either way `grab(a)` returns the `Any` declaration's `Red`.

**The three candidates.**
- **(a) The dispatcher gains the static arguments as parameters**, and every call site the checker resolved with static arguments pushes their RTTIs. This changes the signature of every dispatcher whose least specific declaration is generic, and the descriptor at every call site that reaches one. The template would then carry `X` twice, in its name and in its parameters. The arms would still be stamped through `loadClosureClass` from RTTI names, which keeps the `ZZ32` naming defect (§4). For `grab(Any)` it passes nothing, because that call site has nothing to pass. Not built.
- **(b) The call site loads an instantiated dispatcher named with the static arguments.** It already does, for every dispatcher that is a template (§1). The change is inside the template: each generic arm whose static parameters match the dispatcher's, up to renaming, is renamed into the dispatcher's parameters. It is then tested with a plain `instanceof Sub⟦X⟧` and called as `grab⟦X⟧` by name, and the loader turns both into `Blue`. Nothing is read from the value, and no signature, call site or template kind changes. This is the specification's model, one instantiation of the name fixed at the call, and it is the smallest of the three. Built.
- **(c) The arms keep reading from the value and skip on mismatch.** The template would need `X`'s RTTI in its body (a `X$RTTIc` reference for the loader to rewrite, as trait RTTI classes already get). Each arm would then compare the RTTI read from the value with it. Equality is wrong where `X` occurs only covariantly, because the value's argument can be a subtype of the call site's. The correct test is "read ⊑ call site" followed by instantiating at the call site's argument, and that is (b) with the reading left in. It keeps `loadClosureClass` and both defects of §4. Not built.

## 3. The size, measured

**The shadow** (`scope/scope-shadow.patch`, first file): `OverloadSet.java` only. # The dispatcher taking the call site's static arguments: sized in a shadow

**The answer.** The generic dispatcher is already loaded under the call site's static arguments; only its arms ignore them. Making each generic arm use the dispatcher's own static parameters is one file, one edited function and three new helpers: 43 code lines in `OverloadSet.java`, plus 1 for the switch and 3 for the variant that leaves generic arms out of a dispatcher that has no static parameters. `MieDispatchSub` then prints `Marker[Blue]`. The compiler prelude is byte-identical, and so are the classes of 40 of the 43 compiler tests that declare generic overloads. The other 3 differ only inside a generic dispatcher, and all 43 print the same. Top-level functions only: generic dotted methods fail the same way and are not covered (`ScopeMethod`).

## 1. How the compiled path handles generics today

- A **static argument** is the type that fills a generic's static parameter at one use. In `grab[\Blue\](b)` it is `Blue`. Usually nobody writes it: the checker infers it from the declared types at the call, so `b: Tag[\Blue\]` gives `X = Blue` (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:912-930`).
- An **instantiation** is the generic with its static parameters replaced by static arguments: `grab[\Blue\]` is an instantiation of `grab[\X\]`.
- The compiler writes one *template* class per generic function, with `X` left in the names of the types it mentions (`Marker⟦X⟧`). The class loader stamps an instantiation from it when a class named with real arguments is first needed. For `grab⟦Blue⟧` it copies the template and rewrites every `X` in it to `Blue` (`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java`, `MethodInstantiater.java`). The part of the name after `✚`, the template's arrow type, is never rewritten (`InstantiationMap.java:354`).
- A call that needs no choice at run time is compiled as a call to that named class. The checker's static arguments go straight into the name (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:3670-3735`), so `grab(z)` with `z: Tag[\ZZ32\]` calls `grab⟦ZZ32⟧`.
- **Dispatch** is choosing at run time which declaration of an overloaded name runs, by the argument's actual type. A **dispatcher** is the method the compiler generates for that. It tests the argument against each declaration, most specific first, and calls the first that applies (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1303-1760`). One is generated for a declaration when some more specific declaration of the same name may apply at run time. If the least specific declaration is generic, the dispatcher is itself a template, named and loaded like any generic function: `grab⟦Blue⟧` at the call site (`OverloadSet.java:2005-2062`).
- **RTTI** (run-time type information) is the object every compiled value carries that describes its type. That includes the argument of each generic supertype, one per generic name: `Mixed`'s RTTI says `Sub` of `Red` and `Tag` of `Blue`.
- How a generic arm finds its static arguments today: it asks the value for its RTTI (`getRTTI`), asks that for the argument at the arm's generic (`Sub__1()`, giving `Red`), and passes the answer to `RTHelpers.loadClosureClass`. That call spells the instance's name from the RTTI's own Java class (`runtimeSystem/RTHelpers.java:160-178`, `runtimeValues/RTTI.java:53-58`), and the loader stamps it (`OverloadSet.java:1410-1728`). **What the specification says.** Declarations of one name share their static parameters (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-105`), so "static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable" (`:106-107`). The chapter assumes "that all static variables in functional calls have been instantiated or inferred" (`:136-138`), and they are "statically inferred from the context of the function call" (`expressions/var-ref.tex:37-40`). The call was resolved to `grab(Any)`, which has no static parameters, so the call site supplies none. With no arguments to instantiate it, the generic declaration is not applicable. #!/bin/bash
# scope-run.sh <work-dir>: every command behind ../scope-call-site-dispatch.md, in order.
# <work-dir> is scratch OUTSIDE the repository: shadow sources and classes, private caches,
# the library stack, raw outputs.  No tracked file is modified; default_repository/ is never
# written (every run has its own -Dfortress.caches).  Sections: SKIP_TESTS=1 re-summarises
# sections 3 and 5's saved outputs instead of re-running them (about 90 minutes together).
#
# The shadow: ../shadow/shadow.patch (rung P's -Dprobe.rungP switch and route C's sketch, as the
# dispatch probe built it) on four checker sources, then scope-shadow.patch on OverloadSet.java
# (-Dprobe.scope=off|callsite|skip) and OverloadingChecker.scala (-Dprobe.spSentence=off|own|lifted).
set -u
cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../../.."                     # $FORTRESS_HOME
source experiment/env.sh
M=explorations/reviews/mie-probes; D=$M/scope
W=${1:?usage: scope-run.sh <work-dir>}; mkdir -p "$W"; W=$(cd "$W" && pwd)
CP=$(./bin/fortress_classpath 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
newcache () { rm -rf "$1"; mkdir -p "$1"; printf '\0\0\0\0' > "$1/global.map"; }

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ 0. the shadow
SS=$W/src/com/sun/fortress; rm -rf $W/src $W/classes; mkdir -p $W/classes
for rel in scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala scala_src/typechecker/TypeHierarchyChecker.scala \
           scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala \
           compiler/OverloadSet.java; do
  mkdir -p "$(dirname $SS/$rel)"; cp ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/$rel $SS/$rel
done
patch -p6 -d $SS --forward < $M/shadow/shadow.patch > /dev/null || exit 1
patch -p6 -d $SS --forward < $D/scope-shadow.patch || exit 1
[ -z "$(git status --porcelain ProjectFortress/src)" ] || { echo "ABORT: tracked sources touched" >&2; exit 1; }
java -Xmx2g -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -d $W/classes -classpath "$CP" -encoding UTF-8 $(find $W/src -name '*.scala') 2>&1 | grep -i ' error' 
javac -nowarn -encoding UTF-8 -cp "$CP" -d $W/classes $SS/compiler/OverloadSet.java 2>&1 | grep -v '^Note'

# --------------------- 1. the compiler prelude: stock (the build alone) and under the shadow
prelude () { local c=$1; shift; newcache $c
  local SH="java -Xmx4g -Xss64m $* -Dfortress.caches=$c com.sun.fortress.Shell"
  (cd ProjectFortress && $SH compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss && $SH compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss)
  for f in CompilerLibrary CompilerAlgebra CompilerSystem; do $SH compile Library/$f.fss; done; }
prelude $W/caches -cp $CP
prelude $W/caches-cs -Dprobe.scope=callsite -cp $W/classes:$CP
cmpjar () { local a=$(mktemp -d) b=$(mktemp -d)       # class files of two jars, byte for byte
  (cd $a && unzip -qo "$1" 2>/dev/null); (cd $b && unzip -qo "$2" 2>/dev/null)
  local d=$(diff -rq $a $b | sed -e "s#$a#A#g; s#$b#B#g")
  [ -z "$d" ] && echo "identical ($(find $a -type f | wc -l) files)" || echo "DIFFERENT: $(echo "$d" | wc -l) files"
  rm -rf $a $b; }
{ echo "# the compiler prelude compiled stock and with -Dprobe.scope=callsite"
  for j in $(ls $W/caches/bytecode_cache); do echo "$j: $(cmpjar $W/caches/bytecode_cache/$j $W/caches-cs/bytecode_cache/$j)"; done
} > $D/prelude-compare.txt

# ------------------------------------------ 2. the probes: link under each mode, run, capture
export FORTRESS_CACHES=$W/caches
RCP=$(./bin/run_classpath 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
probe () { local d=$1 p=$2; shift 2               # probe <dir> <name> <flag sets...>

<!-- Scope of the call-site dispatch change, measured 2026-09-23 by a delegated worker on main 20a884410, JDK 25, compiler path. Every run had a private -Dfortress.caches outside the repository; no tracked source was modified. The shadow is scope/scope-shadow.patch, applied after the dispatch probe's shadow/shadow.patch (rung P's -Dprobe.rungP switch): OverloadSet.java (-Dprobe.scope=off|callsite|skip) and OverloadingChecker.scala (-Dprobe.spSentence=off|own|lifted). Commands: scope/scope-run.sh. Captures: scope/*.compiled.txt, dispatch-probes.compiled.txt, javap-template.txt, prelude-compare.txt, compiler-tests.txt, sentence-*.txt. -->

# The dispatcher taking the call site's static arguments: sized in a shadow

**The answer.** The generic dispatcher is already loaded under the call site's static arguments; only its arms ignore them. Making each generic arm use the dispatcher's own static parameters is one file, one edited function and three new helpers: 43 code lines in `OverloadSet.java`, plus 1 for the switch and 3 for the variant that leaves generic arms out of a dispatcher that has no static parameters. `MieDispatchSub` then prints `Marker[Blue]`. The compiler prelude is byte-identical. The 43 compiler tests that declare generic overloads all print the same. Of the 34 that link, 31 have byte-identical classes and 3 differ only inside a generic dispatcher. Top-level functions only: generic dotted methods fail the same way and are not covered (`ScopeMethod`).

## 1. How the compiled path handles generics today

- A **static argument** is the type that fills a generic's static parameter at one use. In `grab[\Blue\](b)` it is `Blue`. Usually nobody writes it: the checker infers it from the declared types at the call, so `b: Tag[\Blue\]` gives `X = Blue` (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:912-930`).
- An **instantiation** is the generic with its static parameters replaced by static arguments: `grab[\Blue\]` is an instantiation of `grab[\X\]`.
- The compiler writes one *template* class per generic function, with `X` left in the names of the types it mentions (`Marker⟦X⟧`). The class loader stamps an instantiation from it when a class named with real arguments is first needed. For `grab⟦Blue⟧` it copies the template and rewrites every `X` in it to `Blue` (`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java`, `MethodInstantiater.java`). The part of the name after `✚`, the template's arrow type, is never rewritten (`InstantiationMap.java:354`).
- A call that needs no choice at run time is compiled as a call to that named class. The checker's static arguments go straight into the name (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:3670-3735`), so `grab(z)` with `z: Tag[\ZZ32\]` calls `grab⟦ZZ32⟧`.
- **Dispatch** is choosing at run time which declaration of an overloaded name runs, by the argument's actual type. A **dispatcher** is the method the compiler generates for that. It tests the argument against each declaration, most specific first, and calls the first that applies (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1303-1760`). One is generated for a declaration when some more specific declaration of the same name may apply at run time. If the least specific declaration is generic, the dispatcher is itself a template, named and loaded like any generic function: `grab⟦Blue⟧` at the call site (`OverloadSet.java:2005-2062`).
- **RTTI** (run-time type information) is the object every compiled value carries that describes its type. That includes the argument of each generic supertype, one per generic name: `Mixed`'s RTTI says `Sub` of `Red` and `Tag` of `Blue`.
- How a generic arm finds its static arguments today: it asks the value for its RTTI (`getRTTI`), asks that for the argument at the arm's generic (`Sub__1()`, giving `Red`), and passes the answer to `RTHelpers.loadClosureClass`. That call spells the instance's name from the RTTI's own Java class (`runtimeSystem/RTHelpers.java:160-178`, `runtimeValues/RTTI.java:53-58`), and the loader stamps it (`OverloadSet.java:1410-1728`). Inside a dispatcher template the arms do this too: they ignore the template's `X`, which the loader has already set to the call site's argument (`javap-excerpts.txt:60-80`).
- The authors weighed the question in a comment: "Some overloads have static args, but even if they are supplied, runtime inference is still necessary (so I think) -- drc 2010-02-24 / Not quite so -- if each static parameter is mentioned in any invariant occurrence, then the supplied type is exact" (`OverloadSet.java:1981-1990`).

## 2. The design

**What the specification says.** Declarations of one name share their static parameters (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-105`), so "static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable" (`:106-107`). The chapter assumes "that all static variables in functional calls have been instantiated or inferred" (`:136-138`), and they are "statically inferred from the context of the function call" (`expressions/var-ref.tex:37-40`). One set of static arguments, fixed at the call, therefore applies to every declaration. A declaration applies at run time if the value's type is a subtype of its parameter type at those arguments. For `MieDispatchSub`, `grab(b)` with `b: Tag[\Blue\]` fixes `X = Blue`. `Mixed` is not a `Sub[\Blue\]`, so the `Tag` declaration runs and the answer is `Marker[Blue]`.

**`MieDispatchAny`'s `grab(a)`, `a: Any`.** The specification refuses the program: `grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])` beside `grab(a: Any)` is "one declaration [with] static parameters and another [without] them" (`overloading.tex:103-105`). The question of which declaration runs therefore does not arise. If the sentence is not enforced, both readings give the same answer. The call was resolved to `grab(Any)`, which has no static parameters, so the call site supplies none. With no arguments to instantiate it, the generic declaration is not applicable. The code should refuse the pair at compile time (§5). Failing that, it should leave the generic arm out of such a dispatcher, which is the `skip` variant below. Either way `grab(a)` returns the `Any` declaration's `Red`.

**The three candidates.**
- **(a) The dispatcher gains the static arguments as parameters**, and every call site the checker resolved with static arguments pushes their RTTIs. This changes the signature of every dispatcher whose least specific declaration is generic, and the descriptor at every call site that reaches one. The template would then carry `X` twice, in its name and in its parameters. The arms would still be stamped through `loadClosureClass` from RTTI names, which keeps the `ZZ32` naming defect (§4). For `grab(Any)` it passes nothing, because that call site has nothing to pass. Not built.
- **(b) The call site loads an instantiated dispatcher named with the static arguments.** It already does, for every dispatcher that is a template (§1). The change is inside the template: each generic arm whose static parameters match the dispatcher's, up to renaming, is renamed into the dispatcher's parameters. It is then tested with a plain `instanceof Sub⟦X⟧` and called as `grab⟦X⟧` by name, and the loader turns both into `Blue`. Nothing is read from the value, and no signature, call site or template kind changes. This is the specification's model, one instantiation of the name fixed at the call, and it is the smallest of the three. Built.
- **(c) The arms keep reading from the value and skip on mismatch.** The template would need `X`'s RTTI in its body (a `X$RTTIc` reference for the loader to rewrite, as trait RTTI classes already get). Each arm would then compare the RTTI read from the value with it. Equality is wrong where `X` occurs only covariantly, because the value's argument can be a subtype of the call site's. The correct test is "read ⊑ call site" followed by instantiating at the call site's argument, and that is (b) with the reading left in. It keeps `loadClosureClass` and both defects of §4. Not built.

- `Tuple.fsi:17-24`: `first`, `second`, `third`, one per arity;
- `QuickSort.fsi:16-20`;

- `Set.fss:76-79`;
- `CovariantCollection.fsi:14-16`: `APPCOV`;

- `Compiled12.invariantInference` (14 pairs) and `invariantInference2` (8), both through `Compiled12.invariantInference.test`;
- `Compiled14`: `f[\T\]()` beside `f[\T extends ZZ32\](x: T)`, through `Compiled14.test`;
- `Compiled16f`: `g(x: String)` beside the functional method `g[\S extends ZZ32, U\](self)`, through `Compiled16.test`;
- `Compiled10.Comprehensions3`: two `__generate`, through `AfterTypeChecking.test`'s `typecheck`;

- 6 are gated: `overloadTest8.fss:33-37`, `doubledOverloading.fss:36-41`, `GeneratorNullPointer.fss:18-20`, `ArrayListQuick.fss:36-55`, `PureListQuick.fss:36-55`, and `genericMethod4.fss:21-22`, whose dotted `g[\T\](t:T)` sits beside `g[\T, V\](t1:T, t2:T)` and which a column-0 grep cannot see;
- 3 are expected failures: `XXXgenericMethod1` to `3`.

`lifted` adds `fmTest3`. `library_tests/` has none.

## 6. Not settled

- **The specification is not uniform on when static arguments are fixed.** `overloading.tex:136-138` fixes them before applicability. `:171-175`, read alone, says of any "call f(C)", dynamic calls included (`:133-136`): "If the parameter type P includes static parameters, they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference} before checking the applicability of the declaration to the call". That is the interpreter's model. The chapter it cites is empty: "This chapter will include the Fortress static type inference mechanism." (`inference.tex:15`).
- **Which static parameters a functional method has.** The specification does not say. `lifted` refuses implementations of a generic trait's functional methods, and `own` does not; this note recommends neither.
- **Whether the sentence covers operators and different arities.** It says "multiple declarations with the same functional name" (`:100-101`), and operator declarations "must satisfy the overloading rules" (`:92-96`). Taken literally it refuses scalar `juxtaposition` beside matrix `juxtaposition` unless the scalar side is padded, and `genericMethod4`'s one- and two-argument `g`.
- **The interpreter, measured in passing** (`walk.txt`). Its overload check depends on names: `ScopeArms` (`Y`) and `ScopeAlpha2` are refused at load, while `ScopeArmsX` (both `X`) and `MieDispatchSub` load. - **Not built:** generic dotted methods, functional methods, `opr` and `nat` parameters (§3). Their size is unmeasured.
- **Not run:** the gate. The shadow's effect on `ant testFast` is not known beyond the 43 programs of §3.
- **The text scan is not the checker** for `tests/`, `library_tests/` and the library components. In a component it also counts abstract declarations, which the checker leaves out.

**The shadow** (`scope/scope-shadow.patch`, first file): `OverloadSet.java` only. In `generateCall` (`:1303`), a generic arm of a template dispatcher gets a `StaticTypeReplacer` from its static parameters to the dispatcher's (`atTemplateParams`). Its parameter and return types are built at those parameters, so they contain no variable of the arm's and take the existing no-inference path. The call goes to the arm's instance named with the dispatcher's parameters (`invokeArmAtTemplateParams`: the same stem the value-reading path passes to `loadClosureClass`, with the arm's name moved away from the dispatcher's as that path does, `:1650-1654`). Code lines: 2 imports, `templateStaticParams` 3, `atTemplateParams` 13, `invokeArmAtTemplateParams` 15, five edited lines in the type-structure loop, and 5 replacing 2 at the call: 43. Add 1 line for the `-Dprobe.scope` switch and 3 for `skip`. `MieDispatchSub`'s template, stock and shadow, is in `scope/javap-template.txt`. Stock reads `Sub__1()` and calls `loadClosureClass` (`:17`, `:28`). The shadow does `instanceof Sub⟦X⟧` and calls `grab⟦X⟧.the_function` (`:68-72`), then the `Tag` generic's own body, `grab♙⟦X⟧`, as the last arm (`:76`).

|---|---|---|---|
| `MieDispatchSub`: `grab(b)`, `b: Tag[\Blue\] = Mixed` | `ClassCastException`: `Marker⟦Red⟧` is not a `Marker⟦Blue⟧` (`scope/dispatch-probes.compiled.txt:21-22`) | `Marker[Blue]`, and `mb` holds `Marker[Blue]` (`:65-66`) | the same (`:108-109`) |

The last four programs mix a generic and a non-generic declaration of one name, which the specification refuses (§2, §5). `skip` is what the code should do for them if they are not refused.

**What else it changes.**
- The compiler prelude compiled under `callsite` is byte-identical to stock, all five jars (`scope/prelude-compare.txt`).
- The compiler tests that declare a generic overload, or match `overload` or `Generic` in the name, are 43 files (`scope/compiler-tests.txt`). Every run output is identical between stock and `callsite`.
- 34 of them link and run. Their classes are byte-identical in 31. In the other 3, `Compiled12.invariantInference`, `invariantInference2` and `Compiled180`, only the generic dispatcher templates differ. `Compiled180`'s last arm, for example, stops re-reading `T` from the value.
- The other 9 fail identically under both: 8 before a jar is written, `Compiled240` in code generation.
- Under `skip`, 42 outputs are identical. `Compiled12.invariantInference` changes: its twelve calls pass `Any`-typed arguments to `f(x: Any, z: Any, y: Any)` beside six generics, and all twelve now print `Any`. Its `.test` expects the run-time answers, so that gated test would go red. The sentence refuses the same file at compile time (§5).

**The remainder**, not built, by site:
- Generic dotted methods. Their dispatcher template comes from `OverloadSet.java:2296-2340` (`generateGenericFunctionClass` with `generateBody(mv, 1)`), with the trait's parameters ahead of the method's (`:2315-2316`). The arms are invoked at `:2240-2265` and the tables named at `:2386-2410`. `ScopeMethod` fails identically, stock and shadow.
- Functional methods in a top-level set. Their static parameters are the trait's plus their own (`:1881-1890`); the shadow guards them out.
- Non-type static parameters. An `opr` parameter has its own naming (`Naming.oprArgAnnotatedRTTI`), and a `nat` parameter needs the size work's run-time kind (FACTS, design A). The shadow guards them out with `KindType`.
- An arm whose static-parameter count differs from its dispatcher's stays on the value path. `Compiled12.invariantInference`'s `[\X1, X extends X1\]` beside `[\X\]` is one; the sentence refuses it.
- A non-generic dispatcher with generic arms stays on the value path unless `skip` is used. The sentence makes it impossible.
- Once the sentence holds and methods are converted, the value-inference block (`OverloadSet.java:1410-1728`) and `RTHelpers.loadClosureClass` (`:160-213`) are dead code.

## 4. The two side defects

**A generic reached through a less specific declaration throws when its return type mentions the parameter.** The value-reading arm ends with a cast to the arm's declared return type, spelled with the arm's own parameter names (`OverloadSet.java:1720-1727`). In a dispatcher that is not a template, nothing rewrites `X`, so the cast is to the template class `Marker⟦X⟧` itself. `MieDispatchAny`'s `grab(a1)` throws this way under stock and `callsite` alike (`dispatch-probes.compiled.txt:31-32`, `:75-76`). The same cast also goes wrong inside a template whenever the arm names its parameters differently from the dispatcher: the loader rewrites only the dispatcher's names. Stock `ScopeArms` casts to an unrewritten `Marker⟦Y⟧` (`ScopeArms.compiled.txt:5-6`). Stock `ScopeAlpha2` gets its `Marker⟦B,A⟧` rewritten with the dispatcher's map to `Marker⟦Blue,Red⟧` (`ScopeAlpha2.compiled.txt:5`). No multiple instantiation is involved in either. **The change fixes it inside templates**: a renamed arm takes the no-inference path, whose call returns the right type without that cast, and both probes pass. It leaves the defect in non-template dispatchers (`MieDispatchAny` under `callsite`) and in dotted methods. `skip` removes that path, and the sentence makes it unreachable for top-level functions, because a set that mixes generic and non-generic declarations is refused.

**A `ZZ32` instantiation made at run time is spelled differently from the static one.** `loadClosureClass` spells each argument with `RTTI.className()`, the RTTI's own Java class: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32` becomes `fortress|CompilerBuiltin%ZZ32` (`RTHelpers.java:174-175`, `RTTI.java:53-58`). Static code spells `ZZ32` as `com|sun|fortress|compiler|runtimeValues|FZZ32` (`javap-excerpts.txt:6`). The dispatcher's value path is its only caller (`OverloadSet.java:1696`). `ScopeZZ32Sub` reaches it through a template with no multiple instantiation. Stock throws: `IntSub` is not a `Sub⟦fortress|CompilerBuiltin%ZZ32⟧` (`ScopeZZ32Sub.compiled.txt:5`). Under `callsite` the arm is named `grab⟦X⟧` inside the template, the loader writes the call site's own spelling, and it prints `SubM[ZZ32]` (`:10`). **The change avoids the defect on the template path and does not remove it.** `MieDispatchZZ32` and `MieDispatch`'s `grab(a)` still throw under `callsite` (`dispatch-probes.compiled.txt:81-82`, `:58-59`), and `skip` removes that path. The two spellings remain: the generated RTTI factories also build class names from `RTTI.className()` (`RTHelpers.getRTTIclass`, `:18-54`, called from `InstantiatingClassloader.java:2810`), untouched and unmeasured here.

## 5. What the specification's overload sentence refuses, measured

**The check.** It is in `checkOverloading`'s pair loop (`OverloadingChecker.scala:383`, before the existing rules; `scope-shadow.patch`, second file, 19 code lines). Two declarations of one name are refused when their static parameters differ in number, in kind, or in bounds after positional renaming. "Static parameters" has two readings for a functional method. Under `own` it is only the method's own list. Under `lifted` the trait's parameters come first, which is how the checker already builds its arrows for a top-level set (`STypesUtil.scala:123-127`). Like every rule of this checker, the check never sees a symbolic operator (`OverloadingChecker.scala:546-550`), and in a component it sees only declarations with a body (`:117-121`). The text scan `sentence-scan.py` counts both apart. On the two library apis it agrees with the checker exactly under `own` (179 of 179, none extra) and finds 326 of 335 under `lifted`.

**The interpreter's library.** `FortressLibrary.fsi` and `RangeInternals.fsi` were checked through the zero probe's stack (`scope/sentence-library.txt`). Two adjustments were needed. The stack's memo hunks are dropped, since the tree has had its own memo since `d28cf74d0`. `QQ`'s `comprises { AnyIntegral, ... }` is written as the zero stack had it, because the tree's form stops the api's check with an earlier error. The stock run gives 203 errors, the triage's figure.
